summary:
The HEARTS Act of 2024 amends the Public Health Service Act (PHSA) by inserting new sections 312A through 312D (42 U.S.C. §§ 244a–244d) to direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to develop and disseminate cardiomyopathy-related education materials, conduct risk-assessment and surveillance activities, coordinate research, and authorize grants for automated external defibrillator (AED) and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) programs in schools. Section 2(b) of the Act provides that no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out these new sections.

Section 312A mandates that the Secretary, in consultation with the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), develop public education materials and resources within 18 months of enactment. The materials must cover: (1) information on signs, symptoms, and risk factors for high-risk cardiac conditions and genetic heart rhythm abnormalities that may cause sudden cardiac arrest in children, adolescents, and young adults, including cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, and others; (2) guidelines on AED placement in schools, early childhood education programs, and child care centers; (3) training information on AEDs and CPR; and (4) recommendations for cardiac emergency response plans. Within 30 months of enactment, the Secretary must disseminate these materials to State educational agencies (for distribution to school administrators, educators, families, and others), to State and local health departments and health professionals, and via the CDC website. Section 312A also includes definitions for “cardiomyopathy,” “school administrator,” “school health professional,” and incorporates terms from the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965.

Section 312B requires the Secretary, through the CDC Director, to submit to Congress within 18 months a report on existing CDC activities concerning the prevalence and epidemiology of cardiomyopathy across the lifespan, including natural history and estimates of emergency department visits and hospitalizations, with public access subject to privacy protections. It further directs the Secretary to develop and make publicly available a cardiomyopathy risk assessment for health care providers and individuals, including a risk-assessment worksheet, a progression worksheet, and screening guidelines, with stakeholder input from patient advocacy organizations, medical professional societies, and federal agencies.

Section 312C authorizes the Secretary, in consultation with the NIH Director, to expand and coordinate NIH research on cardiomyopathy, including causation, long-term health outcomes, and studies using longitudinal data and retrospective analysis, with a requirement to avoid unnecessary duplication. Within 18 months, the Secretary must submit an NIH report to Congress outlining ongoing research efforts and identifying a research agenda for adult and pediatric cardiomyopathy.

Section 312D authorizes the Secretary to award discretionary grants to local educational agencies (including public charter schools) in consultation with a qualified health care entity to develop and implement comprehensive programs promoting student access to AEDs and CPR in public elementary and secondary schools. Eligible uses include purchasing FDA-authorized AEDs, batteries, and maintenance; providing CPR and AED training; developing cardiac emergency response plans; and replacing outdated equipment. A “qualified health care entity” is defined as a public entity or a tax-exempt organization under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code with demonstrated capacity to provide technical assistance in AED and CPR training.
